name: Trait Ascription Bias
description: People tend to see their own behavior as flexible and situation-dependent while seeing other people's behavior as more fixed, trait-like, and predictable. We grant ourselves nuance more readily than we grant others.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to persona creation, research synthesis, moderation, hiring, performance review tools, and internal discussions about 'what users are like.' Teams can flatten other people into stable types while narrating their own behavior as contextual and exceptional.
myth_risk_note: Existing partial backing (Kammer 1982) stands. This pass's search quality was poor -- most candidates were homonym collisions around 'trait' as a general personality construct (anxiety, alcohol pricing perception, trait questionnaires) rather than the specific self-other trait-ascription asymmetry -- a search-tooling limitation, not evidence against the phenomenon.
prevalence_note: Mostly encountered in social-psychology, attribution, and stereotype/perception discussions rather than as a recognizable mainstream UX or product-design term.

findings.description: In a trait-rating study, 56 participants judged their friends' behavior as more consistent than their own while also assigning higher trait intensity to themselves. The result supports the classic self-more-variable / other-more-fixed asymmetry that later discussions call trait ascription bias, while also tying it closely to the actor-observer literature and possible social-comparison processes.
findings.source_title: Differences in Trait Ascriptions to Self and Friend: Unconfounding Intensity from Variability
